title: 22. Interview: Design Instagram
summary: Interview Q&A for Design Instagram — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design Instagram interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 6: Trade-offs & Interview Q&A (5 min)
sections.body:
### Trade-offs Discussed
- **Fanout-on-write vs fanout-on-read**: write gives O(1) reads but O(N) writes per post (expensive for celebs); read gives O(N) reads but O(1) writes. Hybrid is the industry-standard compromise.
- **Cassandra vs Postgres for posts**: Cassandra scales writes linearly but loses relational joins (likes + posts + comments require denormalization). Postgres gives joins but doesn't scale as well. Instagram migrated from Redis to Cassandra in 2012 for exactly this reason.
- **CDN edge caching vs origin**: CDN costs money but cuts origin egress 5× and reduces latency dramatically. Always-on for media.
- **Counter accuracy vs throughput**: Cassandra counters are fast but lossy under high concurrency. Transactional counters are accurate but slow. We pick Cassandra + batched Kafka updates for a 1-minute lag, 99.9% accuracy.
- **ML ranker latency vs relevance**: a complex model gives better relevance but takes > 500 ms. A simple recency sort is fast but boring. We pick a lightweight GBDT model with a 100 ms timeout, fallback to recency.
- **Stories in Redis vs Cassandra**: Redis TTL is perfect for 24-h stories; Cassandra would need a separate reaper. We pick Redis.

### Conceptual Interview Questions

### Q1. Why does Instagram use a hybrid fanout for the feed instead of pure fanout-on-write?
**Answer:** Pure fanout-on-write pushes every new post to every follower's feed cache. For a normal user with 500 followers, that's 500 writes per post — manageable. But Beyonce has 1.2 B followers; one post = 1.2 B writes. Even at 100 k writes/s, that's 3+ hours of work — by which time the post is stale. Pure fanout-on-read (fetch all followees' recent posts at read time) is O(N) per read for a user following 500 people — 500 DB reads per feed refresh, ~500 ms latency, 100× slower than cache. The hybrid: pre-compute feeds for normal users (write-path), but skip celebs and fetch their posts at read time. The threshold (~100 k followers) balances write cost against read latency. Real-world: Twitter used this hybrid for years; Instagram uses a similar approach with a celebrity threshold tuned per shard.
**Visual:**
```
Normal user (500 followers):
  Post -> fanout-on-write -> 500 Redis LPUSHes -> O(1) read per follower
Celebrity (1.2B followers):
  Post -> SKIP fanout -> read-time fetch from poster's recent posts
Hybrid read: merge cached feed + celeb's recent posts -> rank -> serve
```

### Q2. Why does Instagram store the follow graph in Postgres instead of a graph database?
**Answer:** Three reasons. (1) **Access pattern**: the graph is mostly "who follows X" (fanout) and "who does Y follow" (profile page) — these are simple indexed lookups, not traversal-heavy queries that would justify a graph DB. Postgres with two indexes (on `follower_id` and `followee_id`) handles both efficiently. (2) **Consistency**: follows must be transactional (a half-committed follow is a bug). Postgres ACID guarantees this; graph DBs often have weaker consistency. (3) **Operational maturity**: Postgres is well-understood, has decades of tooling, and Instagram already runs huge Postgres fleets. A graph DB like Neo4j would be new operational burden. The trade-off: at extreme scale (1.2 B followers for one user), Postgres sharding becomes complex — Instagram shards by `followee_id % 1024`, accepting that one celeb's followers span all shards. Real-world: Instagram does exactly this; Twitter uses a similar approach with a custom graph store.
**Visual:**
```
Postgres follows table:
  (follower_id, followee_id, created_at) PRIMARY KEY (follower, followee)
  INDEX on followee_id  -> "who follows X" (fanout lookup)
  INDEX on follower_id  -> "who X follows" (profile page)
Sharded by followee_id % 1024
```

### Q3. How does the media processing pipeline work, and why is it async?
**Answer:** Upload flow: client requests a presigned S3 URL → uploads bytes directly to S3 (bypassing our API servers, saving bandwidth) → calls `POST /posts` with the S3 key. Post service writes metadata to Cassandra, publishes `post-created` event to Kafka, returns immediately with `status: processing`. A transcoder worker consumes the event, reads the raw media from S3, runs FFmpeg to generate: (1) thumbnail (square, 200×200), (2) standard (1080×1080), (3) HD (2160×2160), (4) for video, HLS segments for adaptive streaming. Writes outputs to `processed/` S3 → invalidates CDN → publishes `post-ready`. Fanout worker then starts. Why async: (1) FFmpeg can take 10-60 s for a long video — too slow for a synchronous API. (2) The pipeline can retry on failure without the user waiting. (3) The post is created instantly (user sees "uploading..." then "posted"), and the polished media appears seconds later. Trade-off: a brief window where the post exists but media isn't ready — handled by showing a placeholder in the feed.
**Visual:**
```
Client -> POST /media/upload-reserve -> presigned S3 URL
Client -> PUT S3 (direct, bypass API)
Client -> POST /posts {s3_key, caption}
  -> Cassandra: write metadata (status=processing)
  -> Kafka: post-created
  -> return 202 Accepted
Transcoder (async):
  read S3 raw -> FFmpeg -> thumb/standard/HD/HLS -> write S3 processed
  -> CDN invalidate
  -> Kafka: post-ready
Fanout worker: on post-ready, push to followers' feeds
```

### Q4. How do like counts work at 115 k likes/s without overwhelming Cassandra?
**Answer:** Two-table pattern. (1) `post_likes (post_id, user_id)` records "who liked what" — a regular row, supports "show people who liked this post" and uniqueness (a user can't like twice). (2) `post_like_count (post_id, count COUNTER)` is a Cassandra counter table — supports fast increment and read. Each like writes to both. Problem: 115 k counter increments/s on a viral post = high contention. Cassandra counters can have small errors under high concurrency (last-write-wins). Fix: **batched increments via Kafka**. Each like publishes an event to Kafka; a Flink aggregator sums likes per (post_id, minute) and applies batched increments every 60 s. This reduces write QPS 100× and improves accuracy. Trade-off: counts can lag up to 60 s — acceptable for "approximate counts" UX. For exact counts (financial/legal), use a transactional counter in Postgres — too expensive at scale, so we don't. Real-world: Instagram uses approximate counts; YouTube shows "1.2M views" not exact numbers.
**Visual:**
```
Like arrives -> Kafka event {post_id, user_id, ts}
                  |
   +--------------+--------------+
   |                             |
post_likes table            Flink aggregator
  (post_id, user_id)          sums per (post_id, minute)
  uniqueness check            applies batched counter incr every 60s
                                  |
                                  v
                          post_like_count (counter)
                          (lag <= 60s, 99.9% accurate)
```

### Q5. How does Instagram handle a celebrity post that crashes the fanout workers?
**Answer:** Three defenses. (1) **Hybrid fanout threshold**: celebrities (> 100 k followers) skip fanout entirely — no worker load. Their posts are fetched at read time. This alone prevents the crash. (2) **For mega-celebs (>10 M followers)**: even read-time fanout is heavy — every one of their followers fetching their recent posts at refresh time hammers Cassandra. Solution: pre-cache the celeb's last 10 posts in Redis with 5-min TTL; feed service reads from Redis instead of Cassandra. (3) **Rate limiting on feed refreshes**: cap a user to 1 feed refresh per 30 s (most users refresh less anyway). This bounds the spike. (4) **Circuit breaker**: if Redis or Cassandra hit a latency threshold, the feed service returns cached/stale feed with a banner ("Showing older posts temporarily"). (5) **Pre-warm for known events**: Super Bowl, World Cup — pre-cache the celeb's posts 1 hour before. Real-world: Twitter has used all of these for @barackobama and @kanyewest tweets.
**Visual:**
```
Beyonce posts (1.2B followers):
  1. SKIP fanout-on-write (celeb threshold)
  2. Pre-cache last 10 posts in Redis (5min TTL)
  3. Feed service reads celeb posts from Redis, not Cassandra
  4. User feed refresh rate-limited to 1/30s
  5. Circuit breaker -> stale feed on overload
```

### Q6. How does Instagram's CDN strategy work for media?
**Answer:** Multi-tier. (1) **S3 origin**: media stored in S3 (11-nines durability, lifecycle to Glacier after 90 days). (2) **CloudFront/Akamai CDN edge**: 200+ POPs worldwide; first request fetches from S3, subsequent requests served from edge for 24 h. 80%+ hit ratio means only 20% of media traffic hits S3. (3) **Adaptive streaming for video**: HLS segments (.m3u8 + .ts files) — the player picks the highest bitrate the connection supports, switching seamlessly. Segments are small (10 s each), cached independently at edge. (4) **Image formats**: WebP/AVIF instead of JPEG — 30-50% smaller, supported by modern browsers. (5) **Lazy loading**: feed images load as the user scrolls; only the visible 3-4 posts fetch media initially. (6) **Pre-fetch**: when user pauses on a post, pre-fetch the next 2 posts' media — smoother scroll. Trade-off: CDN costs money (~$0.085/GB CloudFront) but cuts S3 egress ($0.09/GB) and reduces latency from 200 ms to 20 ms.
**Visual:**
```
Client -> CDN edge (POP)
            |
            +-- cache hit (80%) -> return in 20ms
            +-- cache miss (20%) -> S3 origin -> cache at edge -> return
Video: HLS adaptive streaming
  player.m3u8 lists bitrates: 240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p
  player picks highest sustainable bitrate
  each 10s segment cached independently at edge
```

### Q7. How does Instagram rank the feed, and what signals does it use?
**Answer:** Instagram's feed ranker is a learned model (gradient-boosted decision trees, possibly deep learning at the top) that scores each candidate post and returns the top 20. Signals include: (1) **Affinity**: how often the user interacts with the poster (likes, comments, DMs, profile views). (2) **Recency**: post age (newer = higher score). (3) **Post type**: user's preference for photos vs videos vs reels. (4) **Early engagement**: likes/comments in the first 10 minutes — viral signal. (5) **User's past behavior**: dwell time on similar posts, save rate. (6) **Relationship signals**: tagged together, commented on each other, DM'd recently. The model runs in < 100 ms per request via feature fetching from Redis + model inference. Trade-off: a complex model gives better relevance but adds latency; a simple recency sort is fast but boring. Instagram picks the complex model with a strict timeout — if inference > 100 ms, fall back to recency. Real-world: Instagram switched from chronological to ranked feed in 2016; the ranker has been continuously refined since.
**Visual:**
```
Candidate posts (~100 from cached feed + celeb posts)
  |
  v
Feature extraction (Redis):
  - affinity_score(user, poster)
  - recency(post)
  - post_type_match(user_pref, post_type)
  - early_engagement(post)
  - dwell_time_signal(user, similar_posts)
  |
  v
GBDT model inference (<100ms)
  |
  v
Top 20 ranked posts -> return to client
(Fallback: recency sort if model times out)
```

### Scenario-Based Interview Questions

### Q1. A user reports their feed is empty even though they follow 500 active accounts. How do you debug?
**Answer:** First, isolate the problem. (1) Is the user's feed cache populated? Check Redis `LLEN feed:{user_id}` — if it's 0 or stale, the fanout workers haven't been pushing to this user. (2) Are the user's followees actually posting? Check Cassandra `user_posts` for the last 5 followees — have any posted in the last 24 h? (3) Is the user's follow graph intact? Check Postgres `follows` table — are all 500 follow edges present? If some are missing, a recent sharding migration may have lost them. (4) Is the read path working? Manually call the feed service with the user_id and trace logs — is it fetching from Redis? Is it merging celeb posts? Is the ML ranker filtering everything out (a ranker bug could drop all posts)? (5) Is the user shadow-banned or restricted? Check the abuse system. Most likely cause: a fanout worker crash left the user's feed cache empty — replay the last 24 h of `post-created` events for the user's followees to refill the cache.
**Visual:**
```
Empty feed reported
  |
  +--> Redis LLEN feed:{user_id} = 0? -> fanout worker missed this user
  +--> Followees posting? -> check user_posts table
  +--> Follow graph intact? -> check Postgres follows
  +--> Read path working? -> trace feed service logs
  +--> Ranker dropping all? -> check ML ranker output
  +--> Replay last 24h post-created events to refill cache
```

### Q2. The CEO wants to add a "live video" feature — how does that change the architecture?
**Answer:** Live video is fundamentally different from on-demand video. (1) **Ingest**: streamer's app pushes RTMP/SRT to a live ingest endpoint (multiple regional ingest POPs). Latency to ingest must be < 100 ms. (2) **Transcoding**: real-time transcoder (FFmpeg with hardware acceleration, or AWS IVS/MediaLive) generates multiple bitrates simultaneously — 240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p. Must keep up with realtime (1× speed). (3) **Packaging**: HLS or LL-HLS (Low-Latency HLS) segments, 2 s each, published to CDN. (4) **CDN**: low-latency CDN config (CloudFront LL-HLS, Akamai Limelight). Viewers fetch segments as they're published. (5) **Fanout**: when streamer goes live, publish a notification to followers (like a post but with a "live" badge). Viewer count tracked in Redis (INCR on join, DECR on leave). (6) **Chat**: separate real-time chat service (WebSocket, like WhatsApp design) for live comments. (7) **Recording**: when streamer ends, save the recording as a regular video post (process through normal pipeline). Trade-off: live transcoding is expensive ($0.50-2/hour per stream); limit free users to 5 min, charge pro users. Real-world: Instagram Live, YouTube Live, Twitch all use this pattern.
**Visual:**
```
Streamer app -> RTMP -> Ingest POP -> real-time transcoder
                                      |
                                      v
                              HLS segments (2s each)
                                      |
                                      v
                              CDN edge -> viewers (3-10s latency)
Notifications: streamer goes live -> fanout to followers
Chat: WebSocket -> real-time comments (separate infra)
Recording: on end -> save as regular post
```

### Q3. A new competitor (TikTok) launches and your CEO wants to add "Reels" — short-form algorithmic video. How do you adapt?
**Answer:** Reels is a different product: not "feed of who you follow" but "algorithmic feed of anyone's content ranked by predicted engagement." Architectural changes: (1) **Recommendation system**: instead of pulling from followed users' posts, the candidate pool is the entire post corpus (or a sample). A deep-learning ranker (two-tower model: user embedding × post embedding) scores candidates. (2) **Candidate generation**: cannot scan all 10 B+ posts per request. Use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) on post embeddings (FAISS, ScaNN) to retrieve top 1 000 candidates, then rank. (3) **Engagement signals**: watch time, completion rate, replay, share — much richer than likes. Captured via client telemetry. (4) **Infinite scroll**: feed is endless, paginated by cursor; pre-fetch next 5 videos. (5) **Video-first**: every Reel is video, requires HLS streaming infra (already have it for IGTV). (6) **Hashtag and audio graph**: users tap on a sound or hashtag to see related Reels — needs a separate `audio` table and `audio_reels` index. Trade-off: Reels cannibalizes the traditional feed; Instagram shows both in the same app with separate tabs. Real-world: Instagram launched Reels in 2020 exactly this way.
**Visual:**
```
Traditional feed: followers' posts -> rank by affinity
Reels feed: all posts -> ANN candidate retrieval -> deep ranker

Reels request:
  user embedding -> ANN (FAISS) over post embeddings -> 1000 candidates
  -> deep ranker (watch time, completion, share signals) -> top 20
  -> pre-fetch next 5 for infinite scroll
```

### Q4. A viral video has 50 M likes in 24 hours and the like counter is showing wrong numbers. What happened?
**Answer:** Two possible bugs. (1) **Cassandra counter drift**: under high concurrency (50 M likes in 24 h = 580/s average, ~5 000/s peak), Cassandra counters can lose increments due to last-write-wins on the same partition. The fix is the batched-increment pipeline (Kafka + Flink) — if it's not deployed or is lagging, counts drift. Check Flink job health and lag. (2) **Cache staleness**: the post metadata cache in Redis might be serving a stale `like_count` that's not being invalidated. Check the cache invalidation pipeline — does the batched counter update trigger a Redis invalidate? (3) **Deduplication issue**: if the user can like twice (uniqueness constraint not enforced), counts inflate. Check `post_likes (post_id, user_id)` for duplicates. (4) **Bot traffic**: 50 M likes in 24 h is suspicious — check for bot signatures (same IP, same user-agent, repeated patterns). If 30% are bots, the count is artificially high. Fix: deploy bot detection, batch counter pipeline, and cache invalidation. Communicate to the user that counts may show "approximately 50M" until reconciliation. Real-world: YouTube shows "1.2M views" with explicit rounding to avoid this exact issue.
**Visual:**
```
50M likes / 24h
  |
  +--> Cassandra counter drift? -> check Flink batched increments
  +--> Cache stale? -> check invalidation pipeline
  +--> Duplicate likes? -> check post_likes uniqueness
  +--> Bot traffic? -> 30% bots inflating? deploy detection
  +--> Reconcile: nightly job computes exact count from post_likes
  +--> Display "approximately 50M" (rounded)
```

### Q5. A user reports they can't unfollow someone — the API returns 500. How do you debug?
**Answer:** Step-by-step. (1) **Reproduce**: call `DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}/follow` with the user's auth — does it 500? Capture the error and stack trace. (2) **Postgres**: the unfollow is `DELETE FROM follows WHERE follower_id=$1 AND followee_id=$2` plus `UPDATE users SET following_count = following_count - 1 WHERE id=$1` and `UPDATE users SET follower_count = follower_count - 1 WHERE id=$2` in a transaction. Check for locks — is another long transaction holding a lock on the celeb's row (1.2 B followers = hot row)? (3) **Sharding**: if follows is sharded by `followee_id`, the unfollow hits the shard holding the celeb's followers — that shard may be overloaded. Check shard CPU and lock contention. (4) **Counter drift**: if `following_count` for the user has drifted to 0 (prior bugs), the constraint `following_count >= 0` fails. (5) **Cache invalidation**: the unfollow triggers a cache invalidate on the user's `following` list — if Redis is down, the API may 500. Fix: ensure unfollow is idempotent (DELETE on a non-existent row should succeed), add retry with exponential backoff, and consider a queue-based async unfollow for high-contention celebs. Real-world: unfollowing a celeb with 50 M+ followers is a known pain point at scale.
**Visual:**
```
DELETE /users/{id}/follow returns 500
  |
  +--> repro + stack trace
  +--> Postgres: lock on celeb's row? (1.2B followers = hot row)
  +--> Sharding: which shard holds celeb's follows? CPU?
  +--> Counter drift: following_count = 0? constraint fails
  +--> Redis cache invalidate failed?
  Fix: idempotent DELETE, retry, async unfollow for celebs
```

### Q6. The Cassandra cluster is at 85% disk and growing fast. How do you reduce storage?
**Answer:** Multi-pronged. (1) **TTL on old posts**: add a 1-year TTL on the `feed` table (cached feeds older than 1 year are never read anyway). Saves 50%+ on the largest table. (2) **Compaction strategy**: switch `posts` from SizeTieredCompactionStrategy to TimeWindowCompactionStrategy — 40% reduction for time-series data. (3) **Compression**: enable LZ4 or Zstandard on tables — 2-4× reduction. (4) **Archive cold posts**: posts with no engagement in 90 days → move to a colder Cassandra keyspace (cheaper nodes, slower reads). (5) **Media offload**: ensure media URLs (not media bytes) are in Cassandra — already done, but check for accidental inlining. (6) **Likes pruning**: `post_likes` table grows unbounded — keep only the last 1 000 likers per post, archive the rest to S3 (rarely accessed). (7) **Stories**: ensure 24-h TTL is enforced (should auto-expire). (8) **Vnode tuning**: reduce vnodes per node from 256 to 64 for faster repair. Net: 85% → 50% in a week. Real-world: Instagram's migration from Redis to Cassandra was partly motivated by storage cost.
**Visual:**
```
85% disk:
  +--> TTL 1y on feed table (-50%)
  +--> compaction: STCS -> TWCS (-40%)
  +--> compression: LZ4/Zstd (-2 to 4x)
  +--> archive cold posts (>90d no engagement) to cold keyspace
  +--> prune post_likes to last 1000 per post
  +--> enforce stories 24h TTL
  -> 85% -> 50% in 1 week
```

### Q7. The CEO wants the feed to be "chronological again" (no ranking). How do you revert?
**Answer:** Reverting ranking is actually simpler than implementing it. (1) **Disable ML ranker**: the feed service already fetches candidates in chronological order (post timestamps). Currently it passes them to the ranker; remove that step and return candidates sorted by `post.ts DESC`. (2) **Pre-compute feed in chronological order**: the fanout worker already pushes new posts to the head of the Redis list (LPUSH) — that's already chronological. So the cache is already in the right order. (3) **Communicate to users**: announce the change (Instagram did this in 2018 with the "Following" and "Favorites" tabs as alternatives). (4) **Keep the ranker available as an option**: some users prefer ranked; offer both ("Default" ranked + "Following" chronological). Trade-off: chronological is fair (everyone sees posts in order) but engagement drops 10-20% (ranking optimizes for engagement, not fairness). For creators, chronological means their posts have a short shelf life — a post 4 hours old is invisible. Real-world: Instagram added a chronological option in 2022 after years of user demand, but kept ranked as default.
**Visual:**
```
Current (ranked):
  Candidates (already chronological from Redis LPUSH)
    -> ML ranker (re-orders by predicted engagement)
    -> top 20

Revert (chronological):
  Candidates (already chronological from Redis LPUSH)
    -> skip ranker
    -> return top 20 by post.ts DESC

No infrastructure change needed — just a flag in the feed service.
```
